comments.author: cole-k
comments.text:
It's a weird time to be alive. Not more than two years ago, most of us here were saying GenAI was no more than "spicy autocomplete" at best --- and fundamentally could not develop further. Now I read pieces like this and this one about math that have shifted all the way to discussing the human effects from them being good at intellectual work.

Now the future outlook seems more like either


GenAI does not advance significantly further, and we're stuck with barely-passable intelligence on tap. In this world, the gap between skilled and unskilled developers widens unless society demands the unskilled developers cultivate the discipline necessary to learn in spite of GenAI. We never reach the promised land and software is just as bad as it ever was. I made similar predictions before, although I think the value of GenAI has increased. One can hope that open --- and especially --- energy-efficient models win in this world, and the resulting industry collapse does not wreck the global economy.

GenAI does advance significantly further, which brings about the world Altman et al. predict and perhaps even desire (the quotes in this article are, frankly, horrifying). I shudder to imagine the consequences. Frankly I hope the techno-optimists are right.

comments.author: pgn
comments.text:
I guess the analogy here is something along the lines of :


Consider a grocery store, the route to which is covered in potholes, snake pits, coyote urine and an assortment of related unpleasantries.

You pay the low low cost of 20$ a month to have Jim Instacartman get your groceries for you from said store.

There is little reason that you would every think "this road needs to be fixed!" unless you experience the displeasure of going through this road, since you yourself are not going down it. If you see Jim suffer, some empathy or sense of "lost efficiency" may motivate you to slightly improve this road, however.


IMO the really dangerous bit is when the road is just bad enough that it's still usable by Jim, but any sane person would realize that it's crap. That's how you end up with cruft accumulating, and the fact that people so readily just offload looking at bad code to their AI of choice is going to make it easier to shit it out (the cost of reading it is paid less and less frequently).

So TL;DR we're probably by and large screwed, at least while discount token rates persist.

comments.author: justinhj
comments.text:
I have 30 years paid coding experience and use AI in my day job. In my position it was already difficult to balance keeping core skills sharp (coding and dsa) when your job involves also a lot of architecture and forward looking decision making and planning. AI could make that worse because the small amount of coding you do is now potentially automated.

However, when we invented powered transport we still walk or jog to keep our bodies working. With code it's the same and I recommend jogging your coding brain by doing one day a week with no AI, or spend some time with leetcode and similar platforms. Take a Coursera course on algorithms. Build side projects.

In the day job you need to balance the acceleration that automated code generation provides with generating too much PR work for your colleagues, and even worse comprehension debt. If nobody read and understands the code, it has no business running customer workloads.

comments.author: condour
comments.text: Certainly doesn't solve the whole problem, but I've been having the agent create a lesson plan and quiz with any complex PR or feature. It's pretty easy to get the model to tune the quiz to the level of complexity you want, have it require scavenger hunts into the code to find specific features, etc. I find that going through this I usually find any major shortcomings with the agent's assumptions about how a feature should work, and other "bad taste" issues. I'm not sure it's enough for a junior developer to get their chops, but it's better than nothing.
